sentences.text: The genus Aoniraptor contains only one known species, Aoniraptor libertatem, which is known from a partial skeleton.
This predator grew to a length of up to 6 meters.
In 2016, researchers identified three unique distinctive traits, or autapomorphies, in Aoniraptor.
The species name "libertatem" refers to freedom and commemorates the bicentennial of Argentina's independence from Spain in 1810.
The front-central tail vertebrae have anterior joint projections without clear articulation surfaces to contact the fan-shaped posterior joint projections.
These front-central tail vertebrae also possess anterior articular projections with a thick, blunt projection on the exterior.
The fossil was discovered in 2010 but was not formally described until 2016.
The central-rear tail vertebrae have paired flattening areas that are not articulation surfaces, located at the upper rear corners of their vertebral bodies.
Phylogenetic analyses classify Aoniraptor as a member of the Megaraptora group.
Aoniraptor is classified within the superfamily Tyrannosauroidea and the clade Megaraptora, but outside the family Megaraptoridae.
Aoniraptor lived between the middle and late Cretaceous, approximately 97 to 95 million years ago, in what is now South America.
The Paleobiology Database records the time range for Aoniraptor as the Albian stage, from 110.1 to 106.3 million years ago.
While the description supports the view that these theropods were tyrannosauroids, other researchers consider them to be part of the Carnosauria group.
It has been informally suggested that Aoniraptor might be a synonym of the theropod Gualicho due to similarities in their tail vertebrae.
